prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose imagination, centred in the Romanian novel and grounded in a lyric poetic base, that turns memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical project.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part, Mircea Cărtărescu (B031). My reasons are the common literary criteria, not the fact that all six round-1 files name him. Chair Olsson's observation that our reasoning and reservations are closely similar, and so may be correlated, is a fair warning that agreement is not evidence of merit. On public knowledge of Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid, his voice is recognizable, and the formal ambition is large and controlled. Memory, the body and dream are built into long architectures instead of serving as ornament. The imaginative and intellectual depth also appears to be sustained across decades and several large books, not carried by one title. A citation can be scoped cleanly to one writer and one language, and it does not need national or political symbolism. The one change in this round is to citation scope. I now centre the citation on the novel and treat poetry as a lyric base, not as a named achievement. The thin translation coverage of the poetry, which Carlberg, Palm and Sem-Sandberg all flag, supports this narrower wording better than my round-1 phrasing. On sustained quality, I accept Sem-Sandberg's standard that a whole-oeuvre prize rewards the peaks and the overall direction, not uniform quality in every volume. I would add one condition: the peaks must be demonstrably several, and the later work must not merely restate them. That is the question I still cannot settle.
statement.case_against: The main risk remains the one I raised in round 1. The achievement depends on density, sentence rhythm and recurring imagery, and I can assess these only through translation and public knowledge. By my own record I regret not being able to read some candidates in the original. Recurrence of imagery may be the method of a metaphysical project, as Olsson suggests, or it may be repetition. Palm, Sem-Sandberg and Sward say Solenoid changes the architecture and widens the field, but none of us has verified this by close reading, and four of us treat it only as a provisional judgment. If the committee's close reading found the late long fictions circling the same material, the claim of sustained, developing depth would weaken. I would then move to Michon (B023), whose concentration is a different kind of achievement, but I would accept that his narrower corpus is a real limit. A second concern is that the shortlist descriptions are brief, and the whole-oeuvre judgment of Cărtărescu rests on a few well-known books. Poetry and early work are the least covered part, which is why I no longer name them in the citation.

responses.point: Palm's provisional answer to the repetition question is that Solenoid changes the mode and widens the field of the earlier trilogy, so recurrence reads as one consistent project. She also says the committee has not yet explained why a few books, as with Michon, would be enough.
responses.response: I accept her challenge on Michon and answer it directly. I can argue in principle that intensity can sustain a whole-oeuvre judgment, because voice and formal achievement are among the criteria and volume is not. But I have not shown that his few books give enough evidence of development or breadth, and I have no way here to verify it. So I do not claim the case is made. I still rank him as an alternative, not as my first choice. On her answer about Solenoid, I find it plausible but I cannot treat it as evidence. It is one reader's judgment, and the chair's question asks what would count as evidence either way. A change in architecture would show in structure, for example in how narrative levels are organized, how the book's scale is controlled and what the book is built around. A mere recurrence of images would not show it. That test needs close reading by someone who can compare the Romanian texts, and I cannot claim that reading.

responses.point: Sward says Michon's slim corpus and syntax, which translation reaches only partly, make a whole-oeuvre judgment more provisional than for Cărtărescu. She says Cărtărescu's long architectures show their method across several large books.
responses.response: I agree that the evidence for Michon is thinner and more provisional, and I take that as a limit on what I can claim, not as a flaw in the prose. The sentence-level quality he is known for lives where translation is weakest. Where I differ slightly is on the symmetry of the argument. Cărtărescu's method is also exposed to translation loss in sentence texture, and the better survival of his large structure is exactly what we are asserting without a verified comparison. I accept the asymmetry as a practical reason for preferring Cărtărescu. I would not present it as a literary verdict that his achievement exceeds Michon's. The preference rests on how much of each oeuvre we can evidence, which is a limit of our access.

responses.point: Olsson treats recurrence of imagery in a metaphysical project as partly the method. He says what matters is whether the later works, Solenoid in particular, change the architecture and not just the motifs. He also doubts that Michon's small corpus gives as secure a basis as a longer body of work.
responses.response: I agree that recurrence can be the method. My caution is that this can excuse any repetition, so the test has to be that the later book reorganizes what the earlier one built. His test fits the chair's question about evidence. I would also answer his point on Michon with a distinction. I do not argue that a small corpus is equivalent to a long one. I argue that it should not be dismissed before the committee has weighed what a few exact books establish. I accept that this is a minority view in the round-1 files and that I have not made the full case. It is why Michon stays an alternative for me and not my preferred choice.

responses.point: Carlberg warns that Nobel's 'idealist' direction is open to broad interpretation and could favour almost any serious writer. She wants the case for Cărtărescu to rest on voice, form and imaginative depth.
responses.response: I accept her objection. In round 1 I leaned on the idealist framework as if it supported Cărtărescu specifically, and the phrase is too elastic to do that work. I keep it only as the background framework, which my own record treats as part of the task along with literary quality. It does not distinguish him from the other shortlisted writers, so I drop it as a reason. The case rests on voice, formal and linguistic achievement, imaginative depth and sustained quality. This also answers the chair's last question: I would not put the idealist direction into the citation.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any source or read any candidate's full corpus. All judgments rest on public knowledge and translation, and I cannot judge Romanian syntax, rhythm and register directly.

Whether Solenoid and later work reorganize the architecture of the Orbitor project or restate its imagery is unresolved. No member has offered a verified close reading, and the supplied record cannot settle it.
Translation coverage of the poetry and early work is thin, so the citation names the novel and treats poetry only as a base. Even this scoping rests on partial knowledge.
Whether peaks and overall direction, not uniform quality across volumes, should be the standard for a late and possibly uneven phase is a committee judgment that I cannot resolve alone.

The alternatives are exposed to translation limits and corpus limits in different ways: Michon's syntax and small corpus, and Wright's limited number of major novels and thinner coverage of her nonfiction.

Shared assumptions and shared public knowledge across the six members may be correlated, so the convergence on B031 is weak evidence about merit. The six-vote structure and Carlberg's simulated vote are modeling assumptions.
statement.conflict_note: No change. No tie to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile, which lists professional ties to committee colleagues and a Gothenburg/West Sweden critical background. My own historical and psychological fiction and my book on Emilie Flygare-Carlén are context, not evidence of preference for any candidate. I disclose that Michon and Wright are my named alternatives, and I note Olsson's disclosure of a thematic scholarly overlap with Adonis and Tawada. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
